entry.title: Combined summary - [BIP Proposal] Stale Tip Relay
entry.summary: The `staletip` proposal introduces a mechanism designed to improve the visibility of stale rates within the Bitcoin network, providing valuable metrics for assessing overall health and diagnosing block propagation issues. This proposal enables nodes to share information about recently observed stale tips via an optional peer-to-peer (P2P) messaging system. Nodes that participate in this system use BIP 434 `feature` messages to signal support, sharing key details such as fork points, compressed header sequences, and flags indicating whether they can provide the actual stale block. Communication is limited to tips within 1000 blocks of the active chain tip, with each message containing up to 20 compressed headers, and each node maintaining a cache of up to 10 recent tips to ensure efficient and relevant data transmission. The effort builds upon AJ Towns' foundational work and has seen collaborative proof-of-concept development by pseudoramdom and w0xlt, with resources available for further review and refinement ([Draft BIP](https://github.com/pseudoramdom/bips/blob/staletip-bip-draft/bip-staletip.md), [Proof-of-concept](https://github.com/w0xlt/bitcoin/tree/staletip-v4)). Monitoring and documenting mainnet stale blocks currently relies on continuous observation by long-running nodes due to the absence of direct recovery mechanisms from the network itself. As a result, documentation efforts, such as those hosted at [this repository](https://github.com/bitcoin-data/stale-blocks), are crucial for research but also raise concerns regarding potential vulnerabilities. These include increased risk of denial-of-service (DoS) attacks and fingerprinting tactics that could compromise network security. The present relay design focuses on single competing branches, which may be insufficient when multiple forks exist, especially in environments like signet and testnets. Such limitations have prompted technical and editorial feedback aiming to better align the feature set with the core operational objectives and safety standards of the Bitcoin protocol. Security analyses of the staletip proposal address possible vectors for DoS and fingerprinting. Existing attack methods already allow peers to send invalid data, and the new relaying constraints—such as limits on branch length and recency—help mitigate risks of resource exhaustion or bandwidth amplification. Nodes maintain autonomy, being able to rate-limit abusive peers or disable problematic features entirely. While enabling staletip does create an observable network characteristic, it remains an optional feature that nodes can disable if the trade-offs are deemed unfavorable. Competing chains are announced distinctly, with each message describing a linear branch, ensuring clear communication regarding blockchain state without introducing additional ambiguity. An incremental rollout strategy is recommended: initially, only stale headers should be relayed rather than full block data. Relaying headers alone captures most benefits, increasing transparency around stale block occurrences and enhancing miners’ ability to respond quickly to reorganizations, all while minimizing disruptions to incentive structures. Full block relay, including coinbase and transaction data, brings added complexity and affects mining incentives more directly; thus, its adoption should be delayed until the impact of header-only relays is thoroughly evaluated. Relay of headers preempts incentive complications while offering robust observability for research and diagnostics. The reference implementation supports three modes—no stale relay, stale header relay, and stale block relay—with "none" as the default setting. Command-line arguments enable user selection, though debate continues about whether relaying blocks should ever be a default or even supported option. Analysis indicates minimal effect on mining incentives from stale block relay: any miner seeking advantage can independently implement enhanced relay solutions, yet the broader reward structure is dictated by cumulative proof of work. Improved relay speeds marginally affect propagation and are more relevant in rare attack scenarios than in typical operations. Relaying both headers and full blocks provides essential transparency during events such as chain reorganizations, dispelling speculation and clarifying network behavior. Several public incidents—including the two-block reorg at height 941880—underscore the value of promptly relaying stale block data to prevent misinformation and confusion, as documented in discussions on [bnoc.xyz](https://bnoc.xyz/t/two-block-reorg-at-height-941880/97/32), [X](https://x.com/wk057/status/2036674054971703361), and [Stacker News](https://stacker.news/items/1460047). Default activation of relaying options is generally favored over opt-in configurations, since their effectiveness depends on widespread participation. If the overhead on node operators is significant, the approach to data collection should be reconsidered rather than simply offering opt-outs. Headers should be relayed by default to capture most advantages safely, while expanding to full block relay warrants further evaluation and consensus. The current equilibrium of the public relay network discourages unilateral deviations by miners, as the costs and coordination required for alternative infrastructure outweigh marginal benefits. Adjustments to default relay behavior produce small advantages mainly in non-selfish mining scenarios and do not substantially alter the incentive landscape.
